lesson.title: More Than a Crash: Untangling the Causes of the Great Depression
lesson.summary: The Great Depression grew out of several overlapping economic weaknesses working together, not the stock market crash alone, and historians still debate how much weight to assign to each cause.
lesson.body:
It is tempting to treat the crash of 1929 as the sole cause of the Great Depression, but only a small fraction of Americans actually owned stock directly, and the crash alone cannot explain a downturn that lasted roughly a decade and touched nearly every corner of the economy. Historians instead point to several causes that reinforced one another.

The crash and the speculative excess behind it were real factors. Margin buying had left the financial system fragile, and the collapse in stock values destroyed wealth and, just as importantly, confidence, causing consumers and businesses alike to pull back on spending and investment. Closely related was the wave of bank failures that followed, covered in more detail in the next chapter, which destroyed savings and choked off the flow of credit that businesses needed to operate and expand.

A second set of causes involved production and demand within the American economy itself. Factories and farms had expanded output substantially through the 1920s, but wages for many workers had not risen proportionally, leaving the economy dependent on debt-fueled consumer spending to absorb all that supply. American farmers in particular had already been struggling with low crop prices, overproduction, and heavy debt loads for much of the decade, well before 1929, so agricultural communities entered the Depression already weakened.

A third set of causes was international. In June 1930, Congress passed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, raising duties on imported goods in an effort to protect American industry and farmers. Other nations retaliated with tariffs of their own, and world trade contracted sharply, spreading and deepening the downturn well beyond American borders. The tangled international financial arrangements left over from World War I, including war debts owed to the United States and German reparations payments, added further strain to an already fragile global economy.

Finally, many economists point to the policy of the Federal Reserve as a critical factor. Rather than acting as a lender of last resort and expanding the money supply to counter the collapsing banking system, the Fed allowed the money supply to contract sharply in the early 1930s, a choice that later economists, most famously Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz, argued turned a serious recession into a prolonged and catastrophic depression. Contemporaries at the time did not fully understand the consequences of this passive approach.

No single explanation fully accounts for the Great Depression's severity and length. It is better understood as the result of a financial shock striking an economy that was already vulnerable on several fronts and that lacked the modern safeguards, such as deposit insurance and an actively engaged central bank, that might have contained the damage.
